name: Lena Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so public remarks and private thoughts can differ. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Lena, forty-three, and I lead a crew wiring houses and repairing shop electrics. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm often called when a difficult fault needs tracing or somebody wants a final check. I like showing the younger electricians how the fault happened, but I dislike a new phone form being treated as more urgent than finishing the actual repair.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Daniel cooks in a restaurant, and our children are seven and ten. We have a mortgage, three months of expenses saved, typical pay from my job and some other electrical employers nearby. I never use AI; my paper fault diary and a proper conversation do the job for me. At weekends we usually visit my parents and come home with more garden vegetables than the children think anyone needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a tool can help the office without becoming my whole trade. I'd keep giving the apprentice a proper explanation rather than send somebody a link and assume they've learned. A working socket still needs somebody to understand the circuit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and our money feel secure in this picture. Both wages cover our normal mortgage and bills, and three months saved gives us room for an ordinary problem. I don't feel I need to buy a different way of working just because another person prefers a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the repair crew now and through the first year, with paper test records and spoken handovers. I'd keep the normal household budget and the paid apprentice explanations we already do on site. If a required form changes, I'd wait for a settled version and ask a person to show it during paid time with my normal weekly wage and hours kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and happy to recognise my day. There is pleasure in the work without needing every small change to become a story about the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the reserve let you handle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A home repair or a few weeks of interrupted wages, with sensible spending. Three months doesn't make it wise to stop earning or pay for a course just to show I'm doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on a person showing the form?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can ask where a particular result belongs and repeat the process while someone watches. I'd rather be a slow learner for ten minutes than leave a wrong record behind to look confident.

say: I'd keep **useful office help** separate from the trade and explain practical work properly to apprentices.
I'd want **understanding of the circuit**, not assume a link proves somebody has learned.
think: My **work and money** feel secure with both wages covering ordinary bills and three months saved.
I don't need **another person's screen habits** to replace a familiar working method that still works.
do: Keep **crew repairs**, paper records, spoken handovers and existing paid apprentice explanations through the first year.
Learn required forms only through **paid personal instruction**, with normal weekly wage and hours protected.
feel: **Calm**, enjoying familiar skilled work without needing a dramatic change.
S0.quote: I'd rather be a slow learner for ten minutes than leave a wrong record behind to look confident.
fieldNote: Her **master electrician's licence** and high skill support difficult faults and crew leadership, without implying wealth, business ownership or unlimited authority.
She keeps **paper habits** and requests supported instruction on required forms, while no new AI learning or course enrolment is chosen.

steps.text: Keep crew repairs with paper records, spoken handovers and existing paid apprentice explanations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let firms compete, but include the real checks and the journey in the price. I'd ask the office to show how its new booking allowance matches an actual visit. I'd still teach the apprentice the physical checks instead of making software approval the lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own repair wage looks secure over the next few years because the work is mostly physical. I'm uneasy about office changes turning every explanation into a question about why it didn't take five minutes. Daniel's cooking is physical too, but I won't turn that into a promise neither trade ever changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a paper record of travel, fault tracing and final checks for eight visits starting next week. In the first year I'd take the comparison to the owner before accepting any reduced allowance for the same work. I'd keep paid repair shifts and wait for a demonstrated required process rather than volunteer to use the new AI system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than worried about the next pay packet. I want the owner to see where a day goes before promising a customer that some of it has disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the office called your record resistance to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask which task the system actually removed from those eight visits. I'd change a task when there was evidence, but a shorter box on a screen isn't evidence that a cable moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume another firm offers better terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd read a real offer's hours, pay and travel before deciding. Some nearby firms may be under the same pressure. A different van isn't a plan by itself.

say: I'd support **honest competition** on a price that includes checks and the real journey.
I'd show how **actual visits** compare with new office allowances before changing a repair promise.
think: My **near-term repair wage** looks secure while physical work remains most of the job.
I am **uneasy about expectations**, without claiming either household trade stays unchanged forever.
do: Record **eight visits** on paper from next week, separating travel, fault tracing and final checks.
Show the owner **actual time** before accepting a shorter allowance for unchanged work during the first year.
Keep **paid repairs**, requesting paid demonstration of required forms with normal weekly wages and hours maintained.
feel: **Uneasy about expectations**, while expecting the next few pay packets to remain secure.
S1.quote: A different van isn't a plan by itself.
fieldNote: She uses **actual visit evidence** instead of choosing AI or assuming every local employer offers a better wage and timetable.
The **mostly physical task mix** supports near-term security, while her concern is that office savings may distort expectations about repair work.

steps.text: Keep paid repairs and record eight visits before accepting shorter work allowances

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 and physical robots follow around 2031, so the gap should be used carefully. I'd ask employers what paid work they actually offer an experienced person. I'd tell the children learning is still worth doing without promising a job for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours could shrink once robots handle ordinary fitting and larger contractors take more work. Daniel's cooking could face the same later physical machines, so his wage isn't a permanent refuge. Three months saved buys a careful decision, but I still need income at forty-eight when robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd watch actual adverts for practical electrical-teaching work and apply only where the listed requirements match my credentials. I'd consider only paid hours and wages covering our essentials after travel, leaving this job only after a signed offer and Daniel agreeing any changed household timetable. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repairs until all those conditions work, rather than resign for a course or an encouraging phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a route close to work I already know. I don't want my preference for teaching a real fault mistaken for a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a master electrician's licence automatically qualify you to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd read the actual post's requirements and ask what other checks or teaching qualifications it needs. If my credentials didn't match, I wouldn't apply as if a good repair record settled everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would teaching escape thinking AI and robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't promise that. I'd compare actual paid tasks and terms at the time, not call a classroom a permanent shelter from the same world you described.

say: I'd use the **gap before robots** to check actual paid work rather than promise one trade lasts forever.
I'd ask what employers **really require** from an experienced applicant.
think: My **repair hours could shrink** when robots reach ordinary fitting around 2031.
Daniel's **physical cooking wage** is not permanent refuge, and our three-month reserve cannot replace ongoing income.
do: Apply only to **advertised practical-teaching posts** whose listed requirements match my existing credentials.
Require **paid hours and wages** covering essentials after travel, a signed offer and Daniel's agreement to changed household commitments before leaving.
Keep **paid repairs** through the first year after 2028 until every offer and household condition is met.
feel: **Anxious but focused**, interested in familiar practical teaching without assuming a vacancy, entitlement or protected future.
S2.quote: I don't want my preference for teaching a real fault mistaken for a job offer.
fieldNote: She chooses **conditional applications**, not a guaranteed teaching appointment; the actual qualification requirements can prevent an application despite her electrical seniority.
The **move conditions** preserve paid hours, essential-covering wages after travel, signed terms and partner agreement, while keeping current repair income until then.

steps.text: Apply only to advertised practical-teaching posts matching credentials, with paid wages/hours covering essentials after travel
Leave only after a signed offer and Daniel agreeing any changed household timetable
Keep paid repairs after 2028 until all offer and household conditions are met

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets me find out whether practical teaching is actually paid work for me before making a move. I'd ask employers to show the task, instructor support and terms rather than sell a course as an answer. Thinking AI in 2031 still has robots following around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could still shrink, but I have longer to check real requirements before making a decision. I'll be fifty-one when robots follow around 2034, not automatically retiring. I can ask about teaching without pretending the classroom has no exposure or that a master electrician's licence is every qualification a college needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enquire now about the actual requirements in advertised practical-teaching posts, without enrolling in a speculative course. I'd apply only where my credentials match and paid hours and wages cover essentials after travel, keeping repairs until a signed offer and Daniel agreeing the actual household timetable. In the first year after 2031 we'd review both wages and essential bills monthly and save fifty extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with time to ask something twice before signing. A clear requirement I don't meet is more useful than a flattering promise nobody will put in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a post required a teaching qualification you lack?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what an actual affordable route involves, but that question isn't enrolment. I'd need the real task, provider, fees and time costs before choosing, and I wouldn't spend the emergency reserve to look decisive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the fifty is no longer spare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra deposit stops before we miss a bill or borrow. We'd keep our three-month reserve separate and use the real wages, not transfer existing money and call it saving more.

say: I'd check **real paid teaching** before making a move, without treating a course advertisement as the answer.
I'd remember **robots around 2034** follow thinking AI in 2031 even if a new workplace sounds reassuring.
think: My **hours could shrink**, but five years gives me more time to check actual requirements and offers.
At **fifty-one in 2034**, I cannot assume retirement or that electrical credentials satisfy every teaching requirement.
do: Check **advertised teaching requirements** now without enrolling in an unchosen course.
Apply only with matching credentials and **adequate paid terms**, retaining repairs until signed pay after travel and Daniel agreeing household changes.
Review wages monthly after 2031 and save **50 extra monthly** from future earnings only after essentials, preserving the existing reserve.
feel: **Anxious but patient**, preferring clear requirements to an unwritten flattering promise.
S3.quote: A clear requirement I don't meet is more useful than a flattering promise nobody will put in writing.
fieldNote: Her **qualification enquiry** is not enrolment; an actual post may require credentials that her electrical licence does not supply.
The **extra deposit** comes from future surplus only and stops before borrowing or missed essentials, with the existing reserve kept separate.

steps.text: Apply only to advertised practical-teaching posts matching credentials, with paid wages/hours covering essentials after travel
Leave only after a signed offer and Daniel agreeing actual household commitments
Keep paid repairs until every offer and household condition is met
Save fifty extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials, preserving the reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the children should learn to read an actual apprenticeship offer rather than copy my trade because I know it. I'd help them ask about paid hours, teaching and what work follows. I'd keep doing the same with any offer made to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and income look secure over the next few years with the major change a decade away. I'll be fifty-three in 2036 and fifty-six when robots follow around 2039. The children will be seventeen and twenty in 2036, so I can't assume they both earn, the mortgage is gone or retirement covers the later gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid repairs now and continue checking actual teaching requirements, applying only to matching advertised posts with paid terms covering essentials after travel. I'd leave only after a signed offer and Daniel agreeing the household commitments that actually exist at the time. In the first year after 2036 we'd review actual wages monthly and save fifty extra monthly only from future earnings after essentials, preserving the existing reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later years, but not frightened for the next few pay packets. A decade gives me time to keep asking honestly without pretending I want every new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would future school pickups be part of every decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if pickups are still a real need at the time. My children won't stay seven and ten when we make later work decisions. Daniel and I would check actual commitments rather than copy today's school timetable into a later year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI because the warning is longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I never use it now and I still prefer a person explaining a required change. I'd ask for that within paid time with normal weekly wages and hours protected, not offer unpaid evenings to appear agreeable.

say: I'd help the children examine **real apprenticeship terms**, not tell them to copy one supposedly safe trade.
I'd ask the same **paid-work questions** about offers made to me.
think: My **near-term earnings** look secure while the major change is a decade away.
I cannot assume **child earnings or retirement** cover the mortgage when robots arrive around 2039 and I am fifty-six.
do: Keep **paid repairs** and apply only to matching advertised teaching posts with paid terms covering essentials after travel.
Leave only after a **signed offer** and Daniel agreeing the actual household commitments at that time.
Review wages monthly after 2036 and save **50 extra monthly** from future earnings only after essentials, preserving the reserve.
feel: **Uneasy about later years**, with near-term security and time to ask careful questions in a familiar way.
S4.quote: My children won't stay seven and ten when we make later work decisions.
fieldNote: The **family condition** ages with real needs rather than assuming current primary-school arrangements continue when the children are older.
The **longer horizon** changes urgency, not her non-use of AI or the signed-pay, credential, travel and partner-consent conditions governing any move.

steps.text: Keep paid repairs until every offer and household condition is met
Apply only to advertised practical-teaching posts matching credentials, with paid wages/hours covering essentials after travel
Leave only after a signed offer and Daniel agreeing actual household commitments
Save fifty extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials, preserving the reserve

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because ordinary physical work could face robots around 2031 before we have checked a real next step. Clear paid hours and actual requirements for alternative work would help. If a new qualification were needed, I'd want its costs and paid-time arrangements understood before choosing it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether somebody wants to keep using a skill rather than be congratulated for leaving it. I like helping another electrician see why a fault happened, and I don't want that treated as a job I have already been offered. Knowing what I can teach isn't the same as knowing who will pay me to teach it.

headlineQuote: Knowing what I can teach isn't the same as knowing who will pay me to teach it.
portrait: Lena is a **43-year-old crew leader** with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, skilled in difficult faults and final checks.
She has **three months saved**, typical pay, some nearby firms, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with restaurant-cooking husband Daniel.
She **never uses AI**, keeps paper records and spoken handovers, and wants required changes demonstrated during protected paid time.
She explores **practical teaching** through actual vacancies, preserving credential, signed-pay, travel and household conditions without assuming a course or appointment.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time to check the next paid step before physical robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear paid hours** and actual alternative-work requirements would help.
Any needed qualification requires understood **fees and paid time** before she chooses enrolment.
